Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. She proved her proficiency in academic English before starting the course. — "Proficiency" đi với giới từ "in" (proficiency in a language/subject), không phải "of" hay "at"; danh từ trang trọng, hay dùng trong ngữ cảnh học thuật.

2. English now functions as a lingua franca between speakers of different mother tongues around the world. — Danh từ ghép gốc Ý, giữ nguyên dạng số ít; thường đi với "as a lingua franca" hoặc "the global lingua franca".

3. Children generally find second-language acquisition easier than adults do. — "Acquisition" chỉ quá trình tiếp thu ngôn ngữ tự nhiên (khác với "learning" — học có ý thức); collocation phổ biến nhất là "language acquisition" / "second-language acquisition".

4. The lecture was full of technical jargon that was hard for newcomers to follow. — "Jargon" là danh từ không đếm được, không nói "a jargon" hay "jargons"; hay đi với "technical/legal jargon" và "full of jargon".

5. Translators sometimes miss the subtle nuances of meaning that a word carries in its original context. — "Nuance" là danh từ chỉ sắc thái tinh tế; collocation thường gặp là "a subtle nuance" và "capture the nuance".

6. Linguists have been documenting the local vernacular of the region before it disappears. — "Vernacular" chỉ ngôn ngữ đời thường, phi chính thức của một vùng; thường đi với "the local vernacular" hoặc "in the vernacular".

7. Hundreds of minority languages are currently endangered. — "Endangered" là tính từ mô tả trạng thái có nguy cơ biến mất; collocation quen thuộc là "an endangered language" và "critically endangered".

8. The debate coach was so eloquent that the judges were immediately won over. — "Eloquent" nghĩa là lưu loát và thuyết phục; cần phân biệt với "elegant" (thanh lịch về hình thức, không liên quan đến lời nói).

9. Many second-language learners continue to grapple with the irregularities of English spelling. — "Grapple" luôn đi kèm giới từ "with" khi mang nghĩa vật lộn với một vấn đề khó; không nói "grapple a problem".

10. Teachers worry that uncorrected errors will undergo fossilisation in a learner's speech. — "Fossilisation" là thuật ngữ ngôn ngữ học chỉ lỗi sai ăn sâu, khó sửa; thường đi với "risk fossilisation" hoặc "the entrenchment of fossilisation".

11. The dialect is now moribund, with only a handful of elderly speakers left. — "Moribund" khác với "extinct": vẫn còn một số ít người nói cao tuổi, nhưng gần như chắc chắn sẽ biến mất; collocation quen thuộc là "a moribund language/dialect".

12. The film's wordplay was simply lost in translation when it was dubbed into another language. — Thành ngữ luôn ở dạng bị động cố định "be/get lost in translation"; không chia động từ "lose" theo chủ ngữ chủ động.
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: Bilingualism confers measurable cognitive benefits on children from an early age. Band 8: What longitudinal studies increasingly confirm is that childhood bilingualism, far from being a mere academic add-on, may reshape the very architecture of a young learner's cognitive flexibility.

2. Band 7: A growing number of languages are becoming endangered as fewer speakers pass them on to the next generation. Band 8: It is the quiet erosion of intergenerational transmission — rather than any single catastrophic event — that is pushing so many of the world's languages towards extinction.

3. Band 7: Machine translation tools still struggle to capture cultural nuance and humour accurately. Band 8: Sophisticated as today's machine translation engines are, they continue to grapple with the nuances of humour and cultural reference that no algorithm has yet fully mastered.

4. Band 7: Bilingual speakers tend to demonstrate greater cognitive flexibility than monolingual speakers. Band 8: Not only do bilingual speakers switch more readily between competing tasks, but they also display a form of cognitive flexibility that appears to persist well into old age.

5. Band 7: When a language falls into extinction, the cultural knowledge embedded within it is often irretrievably lost. Band 8: Were a moribund language to disappear entirely, what would vanish with it is not merely a vocabulary but an entire, irreplaceable way of construing the world.

6. Band 7: Governments have a responsibility to support minority communities in preserving linguistic diversity. Band 8: Only through sustained institutional backing — funding, education policy, and community partnership alike — can genuine linguistic diversity be safeguarded against the pull of dominant languages.

7. Band 7: Adult learners frequently plateau, repeating the same pronunciation errors despite years of study. Band 8: Not only do adult learners commonly hit a plateau, but their errors also risk fossilisation, becoming entrenched patterns that prove remarkably resistant to correction.

8. Band 7: The vocabulary and structure of a language can shape how its speakers perceive aspects of the world. Band 8: Were the weaker version of linguistic relativity to hold, the mother tongue one grows up speaking would, in effect, quietly sculpt the contours of everyday perception.

passages.text: Few statistics in contemporary linguistics have travelled as widely as the projection that roughly half of the world's languages will fall silent during the present century. The figure, first articulated in a 1992 paper by the American linguist Michael Krauss, was rapidly absorbed into United Nations documents, school curricula and international fundraising appeals. A closer look at the underlying methodology, however, reveals an estimate considerably less tidy than its public reception suggests, and the long-running argument over endangerment has become an instructive example of how findings about people and the self can be amplified beyond what the evidence will straightforwardly bear.

The case for the original projection rests, in the first place, on a series of demographic indicators identified by Krauss and his contemporaries. Among them are the absolute number of speakers, the rate of intergenerational transmission to children, and the symbolic prestige a language enjoys in the marketplace, the school and the courtroom. Krauss argued that the convergence of small speaker numbers, declining transmission and low prestige reliably predicted shift to a dominant language within two or three generations. By the early 2000s, Professor Salikoko Mufwene of the University of Chicago was extending the analytical frame, suggesting that endangerment cannot be understood at the level of individual languages but only within what he termed the "ecology of language" — the wider sociolinguistic environment in which speakers make choices about which code to use, when and with whom.

These projections prompted considerable enthusiasm among policymakers and a series of preservation initiatives, some of which proved more durable than the science behind them. The United Nations declared the period 2022 to 2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages, and several governments — most notably in New Zealand, Wales and the Basque Country — invested substantially in immersion schooling and broadcast media. As Dr Alvaro Sandoval, a sociolinguist at the Universitat Pompeu Fabra in Barcelona, has observed, the projection figure became attached to almost every claim about minority-language teaching, even when the original studies had said nothing about classroom practice.

The first sustained methodological challenge appeared around 2014. A research team led by Professor Lenore Grenoble at the University of Chicago reviewed dozens of endangerment registers and reported that the underlying counts were inconsistent, often very small, and apparently sensitive to the definitions investigators chose to apply. What constituted a "speaker" varied so widely across registers — from people who used the language daily to those who recognised a handful of ceremonial phrases — that aggregating across studies might be statistically inappropriate. A subsequent multi-site analysis in 2019, drawing on more than 150 separate community surveys, found that headline projections systematically overstated risk in linguistically isolated communities with strong religious or ceremonial use, where transmission rates appeared to be much more resilient than the global figure implied.

Krauss's intellectual heirs have, in turn, accepted some of these criticisms while resisting others. They concede that not every endangerment claim has been well documented and that some early estimates were probably too generous. At the same time, they argue that lumping all language communities together obscures the picture, because a community shifting from indigenous tongue to dominant national language in a context of urban migration is presumably exercising different sociolinguistic pressures from one whose schools have suddenly become bilingual. The distinction matters, in their view, because the original claims were always about pressured shift, not about gradual diversification. Critics have replied that this clarification narrows the warning to a subgroup so specific that the original public message — that languages are disappearing at unprecedented rates — should be retired or qualified.

A separate and arguably more interesting strand of research has shifted the question from counting to identity. Researchers in sociolinguistics, including Professor Aneta Pavlenko of Temple University, have argued that the more reliable effect of multilingualism may not be on demographic survival at all, but on how speakers construct a coherent sense of self across the languages they inherit. In repeated interviews, late bilinguals — those who acquired their second language as adolescents or adults — report that they perceive themselves as slightly different people when speaking each language. They describe themselves variously as more polite, more assertive or more cautious in one tongue than the other. Such effects are difficult to capture in census-style counts but appear consistently in qualitative research across continents.

This shift carries real weight. When the value of multilingualism is measured in identity and belonging rather than in headcounts of speakers, the policy questions that repay attention are dignity and recognition, rather than dramatic vanishing statistics. A school that values both home languages of its students supports a form of self-recognition that monolingual education cannot easily replicate. The argument, in the writer's view, warrants closer scrutiny than it has hitherto attracted, partly because it is less readily commodified than the headline endangerment claim and harder to capture in a fundraising brochure.

The demographic forecasts, then, deserve to be read with caution rather than fatalism. Fieldwork by the Endangered Languages Documentation Programme in London has recorded cases in which short, intense revitalisation movements reversed declines that statistical models had treated as irreversible. Whether such successes can be scaled remains genuinely uncertain. But the lesson is clear enough: projections describe trajectories, not destinies, and the fate of a language ultimately rests on decisions taken by its speakers, their schools and their governments — decisions that no model can fully anticipate.

audio_scripts.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture moves into our sociolinguistics module, addressing bilingual cognition in the context of language endangerment — drawing on fieldwork conducted across four continents. [pause:5s] The theoretical scaffolding I'll be drawing on comes from the work of Professor Lluis Bonnefoy — that's B-O-N-N-E-F-O-Y, double-N, silent final Y rendered as "wah" in his preferred Quebecois pronunciation. Bonnefoy's 2013 monograph reframed language vitality from a simple speaker-count metric into what he calls "ecological multilingualism theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, some historical orientation. The seminal vitality survey I'll reference today launched its fieldwork in 2010 — sorry, let me correct that, 2007; the published vitality index appeared in 2010 reporting on data collected in 2007. So whenever I refer to the fieldwork baseline, please record 2007. [pause:3s] Right. Moving to terminology. The cognitive advantage Bonnefoy attributes to multilingual speakers — a measurable executive-function uplift in attentional control and task-switching — is termed the "bilingual cognitive reserve". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: bilingual advantage, executive boost, language-switching premium. All of these gesture toward overlapping claims, but they are NOT interchangeable with bilingual cognitive reserve, because the reserve construct specifically references long-horizon neuroprotective effects. The currently accepted scholarly term is bilingual cognitive reserve. So when the older literature uses bilingual advantage or executive boost, just remember they describe a similar but distinct claim. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what fieldwork sociolinguists call the "endangerment severity continuum". When ethnographers grade a language community's status, they sketch a graded continuum running from vulnerable through definitely endangered to severely endangered to critically endangered. So, kinda concretely, you'll see a community where, you know, only fifteen elders still speak the heritage tongue and no children acquire it — that's critically endangered. Or a community where grandparents and parents speak it but adolescents are switching to a dominant language — that's definitely endangered. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the endangerment severity continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the empirical data — and I want you to pay close attention here because the quantifier cluster is dense. Of the three hundred and ninety bilingual speakers we tested across four indigenous-language communities last spring, MOST showed statistically significant executive-function benefit — roughly eighty-three per cent. Only a few — about six per cent — exhibited no measurable cognitive uplift, and some — eleven per cent — showed only marginal advantage. So the cognitive-reserve effect dominates numerically, but the six-per-cent non-responder subset, though small, is theoretically informative for understanding individual variation. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "metalinguistic awareness". This refers to the speaker's conscious capacity to reflect on language structure independently of meaning — sometimes evidenced as early as age four in bilingual children. At Highvale Linguistics Laboratory, our team documented eighty-seven assessed instances of metalinguistic awareness in pre-literate bilingual children during last year's testing cohort. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that all bilingual speakers exhibit the cognitive-reserve effect uniformly is, frankly, not supported. Most of our participants did NOT display equivalent executive-function uplift across attentional control and task-switching subdomains. Quite the contrary — many showed selective enhancement, with task-switching gains dominating over attentional-control gains. So the older "uniform bilingual advantage" hypothesis is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to a tense-orientation point worth flagging here. Bonnefoy's vitality assessment protocol USED TO rely on village-by-village in-person interviewing, NOW the field deploys mobile-application surveys reaching diaspora speakers globally, and from 2029 a multi-agency consortium WILL be rolling out AI-assisted speech-recognition diagnostics. So past, present, future. For today's seminar, I want you to focus on the mobile-survey methodology specifically — that is, the CURRENT protocol — not the legacy in-person fieldwork or the AI-diagnostic futures. So we're, sorta gonna concentrate on the mobile-application generation. [pause:3s] To summarise: language vitality is ecological not numerical; the technical term for the executive-function uplift is bilingual cognitive reserve; cognitive-reserve effects dominate at roughly eighty-three per cent; and uniform bilingual advantage is not empirically supported. Next week we'll examine code-switching pragmatics. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: Growing up bilingual confers demonstrable cognitive flexibility, allowing the brain to switch between mental frameworks with an ease that monolingual peers rarely match.
A high level of proficiency in a second language opens doors to international study and employment that would otherwise remain firmly shut.
Widespread command of English as a global lingua franca slashes the transaction costs of diplomacy, scientific collaboration and cross-border trade.
Early second-language acquisition appears to sharpen working memory and problem-solving skills well beyond the purely linguistic domain.
Learners who plateau too early risk fossilisation, whereby persistent grammatical errors become almost impossible to remediate in later life.
Reliance on machine translation can breed complacency, leaving users unable to grapple with authentic, unscripted conversation.
The dominance of a single lingua franca can quietly erode learners' motivation to master their own mother tongue to a sophisticated level.
Excessive code-switching in bilingual households can, critics argue, leave a child fluent in neither language rather than articulate in both.
Linguistic hegemony tends to arise when one nation's economic and military power allows its tongue to piggyback on that dominance into schools worldwide.
Rapid urbanisation draws speakers of regional dialects away from their home villages, thinning out the communities that once sustained a vernacular naturally.
Colonial history explains why many post-colonial states still default to a former coloniser's language for administration and higher education.
A shortage of qualified teachers and instructional materials leaves many indigenous tongues without the institutional scaffolding needed to survive into the next generation.
When a moribund language finally falls silent, the intangible heritage encoded in its songs, proverbs and place names vanishes with it.
Sustained exposure to two languages appears to delay the onset of certain age-related cognitive declines, according to a growing body of research.
The steady march of linguistic hegemony can leave native speakers of minority tongues at a structural disadvantage in the job market.
Communities that lose their mother tongue frequently report a corrosive sense of dislocation from their own cultural identity.
Governments grapple with the practical difficulty of funding revitalisation programmes for languages that may already be beyond rescue.
Translators and interpreters constantly wrestle with meaning that risks being lost in translation, particularly humour and culturally specific idiom.
Even the most advanced artificial intelligence still struggles to disentangle the nuance that separates polite understatement from genuine indifference.
Speakers of different dialects within the same language family can end up talking at cross purposes, mistaking shared vocabulary for shared meaning.

idea_sections.heading: 5. Problems / Challenges — Vấn đề / Thách thức

blocks.text: Immersive language nests, in which young children are surrounded exclusively by fluent elders, have proved a remarkably effective revitalisation model.
Bilingual education policies that treat the mother tongue and a lingua franca as complementary, rather than competing, assets tend to yield the strongest outcomes.
Digital archiving projects can document an endangered dialect before it lapses into extinction, preserving material for future revival efforts.
Professional development that trains teachers to spot early signs of fossilisation allows learners' errors to be corrected before they harden permanently.
Many parents firmly believe that raising a child bilingual from birth is one of the greatest cognitive gifts they can bestow.
A growing number of linguists contend that linguistic diversity is as worth safeguarding as biological diversity, given how much irreplaceable ecological knowledge it encodes.
Some members of the public assume that an eloquent speaker is automatically more intelligent, a conflation that linguists are quick to dispute.
There is widespread, if contested, sympathy for the view that funding endangered languages amounts to a financial burden better spent elsewhere.

idea_sections.heading: 7. Popular opinions — Quan điểm phổ biến

blocks.text: National governments bear primary responsibility for enshrining minority-language rights in education policy rather than leaving revitalisation to grassroots volunteers alone.
International bodies such as UNESCO play a coordinating role, cataloguing endangered languages and channelling expertise to communities that request it.
Parents and elders within a speech community hold a unique duty to transmit the mother tongue to children before it lapses into disuse.
Technology firms developing translation software arguably owe it to smaller language communities to grapple with low-resource dialects rather than focusing solely on commercially lucrative markets.

idea_sections.heading: 8. Who is responsible — Trách nhiệm thuộc về ai

blocks.text: While critics dismiss preservation funding as a financial burden, proponents counter that the intangible heritage at stake is, by definition, irreplaceable once lost.

Although some maintain that language death is simply an inevitable historical process, akin to Latin's evolution, opponents note that Latin's descendants survived, unlike many truly moribund tongues today.
Sceptics of the strong version of linguistic relativity argue that thought is not straightforwardly imprisoned by grammar, though a moderated version still commands considerable empirical support.
It could be argued that a universal lingua franca promotes peace and efficiency, yet this claim has come under growing scrutiny from scholars who see it as a euphemism for linguistic hegemony.
Artificial intelligence is likely to narrow, though not eliminate, the gap between machine and human translation, particularly for content once routinely lost in translation.
As remote work expands, demand for proficiency in a shared lingua franca is set to intensify across industries that were previously insulated from global competition.
Growing awareness of linguistic diversity as cultural capital may push more governments to treat revitalisation as a matter of prestige rather than financial burden alone.
Without concerted intervention, linguists warn that a substantial proportion of the world's languages could edge closer to extinction within a few generations.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas a dialect remains mutually intelligible with its parent language, a fully endangered minority language may already be unintelligible to speakers of the dominant tongue nearby.
Compared with adult learners, who often battle fossilisation, young children acquire native-like command of a second language with comparatively little conscious effort.
Unlike the vernacular spoken casually at home, the formal register taught in classrooms is typically far more standardised and rule-bound.
Whereas machine translation excels at literal, high-frequency vocabulary, human interpreters remain indispensable for capturing the nuance of humour, sarcasm and cultural allusion.
The successful revitalisation of Welsh and Maori through language nests and state-funded broadcasting is frequently cited as proof that reviving a moribund tongue is achievable.
Longitudinal studies comparing bilingual and monolingual adults offer some of the most persuasive evidence for lasting cognitive flexibility benefits.
Anecdotes from professional interpreters, who routinely admit that certain jokes are simply lost in translation, illustrate the practical limits of even highly skilled human translation.
UNESCO's periodically updated atlas of endangered languages provides a widely cited evidence base for tracking global linguistic diversity and its decline.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: It is a striking fact that one minority language disappears roughly every two weeks. Whether such losses ought to be accepted as a natural evolution or actively resisted through preservation efforts is a question that divides linguists and policymakers. This essay will examine both views before arguing that determined preservation is, on balance, the wiser course.

Those who advocate letting minority languages die out argue that language extinction has always been part of human history. Latin, for example, gave way to the Romance languages without humanity being culturally impoverished by the change. From this perspective, attempting to artificially preserve every endangered dialect is a costly exercise that may yield little practical return. Furthermore, in an increasingly interconnected world, a young speaker of a minority tongue often gains far more economically from acquiring proficiency in a dominant lingua franca than from retaining a dialect of limited reach.

On the other hand, the case for preservation is, to my mind, the stronger one. Each language encodes unique ecological and historical knowledge; when it vanishes, that knowledge is lost forever. Moreover, a mother tongue is bound up with cultural identity, so its disappearance can inflict real psychological harm on a community. Crucially, revival is feasible rather than merely aspirational: Welsh, Maori and Hebrew have all been successfully revitalised through state-funded schooling, broadcasting and community language programmes.

In conclusion, although language death is sometimes a natural process, the cultural and intellectual cost of inaction is simply too high. Governments should therefore fund the targeted preservation of viable minority languages, prioritising those with a realistic prospect of survival, rather than allow them all to fall into extinction unchecked.

It is a sobering statistic that an indigenous language slips into extinction roughly every fortnight. Whether such attrition should be accepted as the natural churn of history or contested through deliberate preservation is a question that sharply divides scholars. My own position, on balance, is that selective preservation is amply justified, even if not every dialect can realistically be rescued.

There is, admittedly, a coherent case for non-intervention. Languages have always evolved, merged and died: Latin dissolved into the Romance tongues with no discernible loss to human civilisation, which suggests that propping up every moribund variety may be quixotic. Compounding this is the matter of cost; funds poured into reviving languages with a handful of elderly speakers might, some contend, be more humanely spent on healthcare or schooling. For the individual learner, moreover, fluency in a dominant lingua franca yields economic returns that a minority dialect simply cannot match.

Persuasive as these arguments are, they understate what is forfeited. Each language constitutes a unique repository of ecological and medicinal knowledge, much of it absent from any written archive; its loss is therefore irreversible. More fundamentally, a mother tongue is constitutive of cultural identity, which is precisely why UNESCO frames linguistic erasure as a form of cultural violence. And revival, far from being utopian, is demonstrable: were sustained funding married to grassroots transmission, even severely endangered languages could be resurrected, as Hebrew, Welsh and Maori attest.

In sum, while language death is partly inevitable, passive resignation is not the only response. The wiser course is to channel finite resources toward languages with a viable speaker community and a documented prospect of transmission, thereby preserving irreplaceable heritage without indulging in the futile fantasy of universal rescue.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. She proved her proficiency in academic English before starting the course. — "Proficiency" đi với giới từ "in" (proficiency in a language/subject), không phải "of" hay "at"; danh từ trang trọng, hay dùng trong ngữ cảnh học thuật.

2. English now functions as a lingua franca between speakers of different mother tongues around the world. — Danh từ ghép gốc Ý, giữ nguyên dạng số ít; thường đi với "as a lingua franca" hoặc "the global lingua franca".

3. Children generally find second-language acquisition easier than adults do. — "Acquisition" chỉ quá trình tiếp thu ngôn ngữ tự nhiên (khác với "learning" — học có ý thức); collocation phổ biến nhất là "language acquisition" / "second-language acquisition".

4. The lecture was full of technical jargon that was hard for newcomers to follow. — "Jargon" là danh từ không đếm được, không nói "a jargon" hay "jargons"; hay đi với "technical/legal jargon" và "full of jargon".

5. Translators sometimes miss the subtle nuances of meaning that a word carries in its original context. — "Nuance" là danh từ chỉ sắc thái tinh tế; collocation thường gặp là "a subtle nuance" và "capture the nuance".

6. Linguists have been documenting the local vernacular of the region before it disappears. — "Vernacular" chỉ ngôn ngữ đời thường, phi chính thức của một vùng; thường đi với "the local vernacular" hoặc "in the vernacular".

7. Hundreds of minority languages are currently endangered. — "Endangered" là tính từ mô tả trạng thái có nguy cơ biến mất; collocation quen thuộc là "an endangered language" và "critically endangered".

8. The debate coach was so eloquent that the judges were immediately won over. — "Eloquent" nghĩa là lưu loát và thuyết phục; cần phân biệt với "elegant" (thanh lịch về hình thức, không liên quan đến lời nói).

9. Many second-language learners continue to grapple with the irregularities of English spelling. — "Grapple" luôn đi kèm giới từ "with" khi mang nghĩa vật lộn với một vấn đề khó; không nói "grapple a problem".

10. Teachers worry that uncorrected errors will undergo fossilisation in a learner's speech. — "Fossilisation" là thuật ngữ ngôn ngữ học chỉ lỗi sai ăn sâu, khó sửa; thường đi với "risk fossilisation" hoặc "the entrenchment of fossilisation".

11. The dialect is now moribund, with only a handful of elderly speakers left. — "Moribund" khác với "extinct": vẫn còn một số ít người nói cao tuổi, nhưng gần như chắc chắn sẽ biến mất; collocation quen thuộc là "a moribund language/dialect".

12. The film's wordplay was simply lost in translation when it was dubbed into another language. — Thành ngữ luôn ở dạng bị động cố định "be/get lost in translation"; không chia động từ "lose" theo chủ ngữ chủ động.
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: Bilingualism confers measurable cognitive benefits on children from an early age. Band 8: What longitudinal studies increasingly confirm is that childhood bilingualism, far from being a mere academic add-on, may reshape the very architecture of a young learner's cognitive flexibility.

2. Band 7: A growing number of languages are becoming endangered as fewer speakers pass them on to the next generation. Band 8: It is the quiet erosion of intergenerational transmission — rather than any single catastrophic event — that is pushing so many of the world's languages towards extinction.

3. Band 7: Machine translation tools still struggle to capture cultural nuance and humour accurately. Band 8: Sophisticated as today's machine translation engines are, they continue to grapple with the nuances of humour and cultural reference that no algorithm has yet fully mastered.

4. Band 7: Bilingual speakers tend to demonstrate greater cognitive flexibility than monolingual speakers. Band 8: Not only do bilingual speakers switch more readily between competing tasks, but they also display a form of cognitive flexibility that appears to persist well into old age.

5. Band 7: When a language falls into extinction, the cultural knowledge embedded within it is often irretrievably lost. Band 8: Were a moribund language to disappear entirely, what would vanish with it is not merely a vocabulary but an entire, irreplaceable way of construing the world.

6. Band 7: Governments have a responsibility to support minority communities in preserving linguistic diversity. Band 8: Only through sustained institutional backing — funding, education policy, and community partnership alike — can genuine linguistic diversity be safeguarded against the pull of dominant languages.

7. Band 7: Adult learners frequently plateau, repeating the same pronunciation errors despite years of study. Band 8: Not only do adult learners commonly hit a plateau, but their errors also risk fossilisation, becoming entrenched patterns that prove remarkably resistant to correction.

8. Band 7: The vocabulary and structure of a language can shape how its speakers perceive aspects of the world. Band 8: Were the weaker version of linguistic relativity to hold, the mother tongue one grows up speaking would, in effect, quietly sculpt the contours of everyday perception.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
The Rate of Language Extinction: Linguists estimate that one indigenous language dies every two weeks. By the end of this century, nearly half of the world's 7,000 languages may disappear.
The Rise of AI Translation: Tools like Google Translate and DeepL have achieved near-human accuracy for literal translation, but they still fail at semantics, humor, and cultural colloquialisms.
Cognitive Benefits of Bilingualism: Studies show that second language acquisition delays the onset of dementia and improves multitasking and problem-solving skills.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: A Single Global Language (Should everyone speak the same language?)

Arguments FOR (Pros): Removes the language barrier, boosting international trade and scientific collaboration; reduces misunderstandings and prevents global conflicts (promotes peace); significantly cuts the costs of translation services in organisations like the UN.

Arguments AGAINST (Cons): Language is inextricably linked to cultural identity—a single language would lead to cultural homogenisation; it gives native speakers of the global language an unfair economic and educational advantage; causes the tragic extinction of minority dialects and traditional folklore.
Topic: Translation Technology vs. Human Learning
Technology Pros: Instantly accessible and cheap; breaks down immediate communication barriers for tourists and basic business transactions; eliminates the need for years of rigorous grammar study.

Learning Pros: Machines cannot translate human empathy, tone, or cultural etiquette; learning a language builds cognitive resilience; true bilingualism allows for deep, authentic cross-cultural connections that a screen cannot replicate.
Topic: Preserving Minority Languages (Should governments fund it?)

Arguments FOR: Languages contain unique ecological and historical knowledge (intangible heritage); losing a mother tongue is a loss of human diversity; funds can be used to revitalize dialects through school curriculums.

Arguments AGAINST: It is a massive financial burden; it is more practical to teach youths a dominant lingua franca to secure their economic future; languages naturally evolve and die out—it is an inevitable historical process.
(Đảo ngữ Câu điều kiện - Cấu trúc siêu học thuật giúp bạn gây ấn tượng mạnh với Giám khảo trong các bài luận về Đề xuất Giải pháp hoặc Giả định Hệ quả)

Normal: If they had preserved the dialect, it wouldn't have died.
Inversion: Had they preserved the dialect, it wouldn't have died.

Model Answer (272 words)

The language I've genuinely wrestled with — and continue to, in all candour — is Mandarin Chinese, a tongue I began studying roughly two years ago when my company expanded its operations into Shenzhen. (hedging)
What initially drew me in was the prospect of unmediated conversations with our manufacturing partners, but what kept me hooked was the sheer alien beauty of the script and tonal system. (cleft)

The acquisition of Mandarin has, by any objective measure, been the steepest linguistic climb I've undertaken. (nominalisation) For a native Vietnamese speaker, the tones are admittedly more navigable than for a European learner, yet the absence of cognates with English, combined with a logographic writing system requiring rote memorisation of thousands of characters, made early progress glacial. Worse still, I noticed I was beginning to suffer from what linguists term fossilisation — the entrenchment of recurring errors that resist remediation. (reduced relative)

Were I to start again from scratch, I would prioritise immersive listening from day one. (conditional inversion) As it stands, my strategy has been multi-pronged: a daily one-hour language exchange with a Beijing-based partner, Anki-style spaced repetition for vocabulary retention, and a deliberate strategy of shadowing native podcasts. Not only did this approach rekindle my motivation, but it also leveraged the brain's neuroplasticity more effectively than textbook study ever did. (negative inversion)

It is the cumulative effect of micro-habits, rather than any single breakthrough, that has gradually nudged me towards conversational proficiency. (cleft) I'm still a long way from being fluent (informal idiom), and tonal subtleties routinely trip me up (informal idiom), but I'm closer than I was eighteen months ago — and that, frankly, is enough.
Examiner Follow-up
"Would you recommend Mandarin to other learners?"

Suggested response (40 words): Honestly, it depends on motivation. Were one to learn purely for travel, the return on investment is dubious. But for anyone in trade, manufacturing, or East-Asian academia, the dividends are substantial — provided you commit for the long haul.

blocks.text: Q1. Should English remain the global lingua franca?
P: English's current status as the global lingua franca is, on balance, a pragmatic asset — though one that demands honest reckoning with the inequities it perpetuates.
E: A shared global language lubricates trade, science, and diplomacy, but it also confers structural advantages on native speakers and accelerates the marginalisation of minority tongues.

E: British Council (2023) estimates that some 1.75 billion people worldwide now speak English to a useful level — roughly one in four humans. Ethnologue (2023) ranks English as the most studied second language globally. Yet UNESCO (2022) documents that English-medium higher education is correlated with declining usage of indigenous academic vocabularies. Meanwhile, Jennifer Jenkins' English as a Lingua Franca (ELF) research programme and Barbara Seidlhofer's VOICE corpus work (University of Vienna) consistently find that non-native interlocutors in international settings often outperform native speakers in mutual intelligibility precisely because they avoid culture-bound idiomatic ambiguity — a point David Crystal's English as a Global Language (2003) had already foreshadowed.

L: Therefore, English should remain the working lingua franca, but active linguistic accommodation — clearer English, multilingual subtitling, AI-augmented translation — must mitigate its hegemonic effects.
Hedging Toolbox: with appropriate qualifications / one might reasonably contend / for the foreseeable future
Lexical Upgrade Box:
world language → lingua franca / global vehicular language
spread → proliferation / linguistic hegemony
useful → pragmatically indispensable
Sample Answer (95 words):

For the foreseeable future, English should remain the global lingua franca — but with qualifications. British Council (2023) estimates 1.75 billion English users globally, and Ethnologue (2023) confirms its dominance in international communication. However, what's often overlooked is the inequity: UNESCO (2022) flagged that English-medium tertiary education erodes indigenous academic vocabularies. Were policy to mandate multilingual subtitling and AI-augmented translation in international fora, the hegemonic effects could be substantially mitigated. Not only does this preserve English's utility, but it also dilutes the unfair advantage native speakers currently enjoy — a fair compromise.
Q2. Is it possible to revive extinct languages?

P: Full revival of a truly extinct language is vanishingly rare, but partial reconstruction and the revitalisation of moribund languages are demonstrably achievable, given sustained political and community commitment.

E: The distinction matters: an extinct language has zero living speakers, whereas a moribund language has elderly speakers and a thin documentary record — the latter offering a viable revival corridor.

E: Modern Hebrew stands as the most spectacular case: from a purely liturgical language with no native speakers in the 19th century to roughly 9 million native speakers today (Ethnologue, 2023) following Eliezer Ben-Yehuda's deliberate revivalist project. Cornish, declared extinct in 1777, has been partially reconstructed and now has roughly 500 fluent speakers (Cornwall Council, 2021). UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger (2023) lists revival success cases including Welsh and Māori, the latter with state-funded kōhanga reo language nests.
L: Hence, while revival is resource-intensive and rarely complete, dismissing it as impossible flies in the face of documented success stories.
Hedging Toolbox: the evidence broadly indicates / to a meaningful extent / with sufficient institutional backing
Lexical Upgrade Box:
bring back → revitalise / resurrect
die out → fall into extinction / become moribund
speakers → the speaker community / native users
Sample Answer (95 words):

The evidence broadly indicates that revival is genuinely possible, though resource-intensive. Modern Hebrew is the most striking case: from a purely liturgical language in the 1880s to 9 million native speakers today (Ethnologue, 2023). Cornish, declared extinct in 1777, now has roughly 500 fluent speakers thanks to deliberate reconstruction. Were sufficient state funding combined with grassroots transmission, even severely endangered languages — as documented in UNESCO's 2023 Atlas — could plausibly be revived. Not only does this preserve intangible heritage, but it also restores cultural agency to marginalised communities — an outcome with measurable psychological benefits.
Q3. How does language shape thinking?

P: Language shapes cognition in ways that are measurable but bounded — a moderated version of the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis is now empirically defensible, though strong linguistic determinism has been largely discredited.
E: The grammatical and lexical structures of one's mother tongue predispose, rather than determine, how speakers attend to colour, space, time, and agency.

E: Lera Boroditsky's research at Stanford (2011, 2020) demonstrated that Russian speakers, whose language distinguishes light and dark blue lexically, discriminate these shades faster than English speakers. The Pirahã of the Amazon, lacking exact number words beyond "two", show measurable difficulty with precise numerical tasks (Frank et al., MIT, 2008). Meanwhile, APA-published meta-analyses (2019) confirm bilinguals exhibit enhanced cognitive flexibility and slower onset of dementia by roughly 4 years (Bialystok et al., 2012, 2020).
L: Therefore, language doesn't imprison thought, but it does sculpt the cognitive terrain in which thought unfolds — a far more interesting conclusion than either extreme.
Hedging Toolbox: the converging evidence suggests / in a qualified sense / not in any deterministic way
Lexical Upgrade Box:
change thinking → shape cognition / sculpt cognitive terrain
people → speakers / language users
brain → cognitive processes / neural architecture
Sample Answer (96 words):

The converging evidence suggests language shapes thinking in a qualified sense. Boroditsky's Stanford research (2011, 2020) showed Russian speakers, whose language lexicalises light and dark blue separately, discriminate these shades faster than English speakers. The Pirahã, who lack precise number words, show measurable numerical-cognition limits (Frank et al., MIT, 2008). APA meta-analyses (2019) also confirm bilinguals show enhanced cognitive flexibility and delayed dementia onset by roughly four years. Were the strong Sapir-Whorf hypothesis correct, translation would be impossible — yet it isn't. So language sculpts cognition without imprisoning it — a far more nuanced reality.
T07 — LANGUAGE & LINGUISTICS (Advanced C1, Band 7.5–8.0)
1. Section Type + Lecturer Info
Section: IELTS Listening Section 4 — single-speaker academic lecture, no audience interaction
Lecturer: Professor Linh Tran-Hayward, applied linguist
Academic field: Sociolinguistics / Cognitive Linguistics
Topic of lecture: "Language Extinction, Linguistic Relativity and the Cognitive Dividends of Bilingualism"
2. Pre-listening Vocab Brush-up (Band 7+)
lingua franca (n phrase) — a common language adopted between speakers of different mother tongues
linguistic relativity (n phrase) — the hypothesis that language shapes thought (Sapir-Whorf)
bilingualism (n) — fluency in two languages
proficiency (n) — high level of mastery of a skill, especially a language
fossilisation (n) — permanent settling of errors in second-language learners
3. Predict 3 Ideas (Advanced)
The lecturer will likely argue that language extinction is accelerating at an alarming rate worldwide.
She may discuss linguistic relativity — the idea that the language we speak shapes how we perceive the world.
Evidence for the cognitive benefits of bilingualism, perhaps delayed onset of dementia, will probably feature.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

Good afternoon. Today's lecture knits together three of the most contested debates in applied linguistics: the accelerating crisis of language extinction, the much-debated thesis of linguistic relativity, and finally the cognitive dividends of bilingualism. [pause]

Let's begin with the numbers. Of the roughly seven thousand languages currently spoken, linguists project that nearly half will fall silent by the close of this century. To put it more starkly, one indigenous tongue disappears every fortnight. Now, this isn't merely sentimental loss — each extinct language takes with it ecological knowledge, oral history and, indeed, a particular cognitive lens. [pause]

This brings us neatly to linguistic relativity, often associated with Sapir and Whorf. The strong version — that language determines thought entirely — has been, um, largely discredited. However, the weaker version retains considerable empirical support: speakers of languages with finer colour vocabularies, for instance, demonstrably distinguish hues more rapidly. So language doesn't imprison thought, but it does, in a real sense, channel it. [pause]

Now, the cognitive payoffs of bilingualism are perhaps the most actionable finding for educators. Longitudinal studies — notably Bialystok's work in Toronto — indicate that lifelong bilinguals exhibit delayed onset of dementia by, on average, four to five years. Moreover, bilingual children consistently outperform monolingual peers on tasks requiring executive function and cognitive flexibility. [pause]

One caveat, however. The benefits accrue only when proficiency in both languages is genuinely high. Superficial exposure — what we sometimes call passive bilingualism — confers, frankly, negligible advantage. And learners who plateau too early risk fossilisation, whereby errors crystallise and become extraordinarily resistant to correction. [pause]

Now, having said all that, I'd be doing you a disservice if I left the bilingual-advantage thesis looking quite so unassailable, because in recent years it has come under genuinely fierce scrutiny. Let me bring in the counter-evidence. A replication study led by Kenneth Paap reviewed a swathe of executive-function experiments and found that the much-trumpeted bilingual advantage shrank dramatically, or vanished entirely, once you controlled for publication bias — that is, the tendency of journals to print positive results and quietly bury the null findings. Paap rather provocatively called it an effect that exists "in the lab but not in life". So, um, intellectual honesty obliges me to say the jury is, at the very least, reconvened. [pause]

What complicates this further is the confound of socioeconomic status. Many of the most cited bilingual cohorts were, frankly, affluent and highly educated — and we know independently that affluence buffers cognitive decline. So how much of Bialystok's dementia-delay is bilingualism per se, and how much is simply the cognitive reserve that comes with a richer environment? Disentangling the two is fiendishly difficult, and the field is only now designing studies with the controls to do it. [pause]

A further nuance worth flagging concerns language extinction, where the politics are sharper than the sentiment suggests. Revival is not merely about recording vocabulary in a database. Hebrew's resurrection succeeded because it was yoked to statehood and daily necessity; Cornish and Manx limp along precisely because they lack that functional engine. A language survives, if you like, only when it has somewhere to be spoken — a school, a marketplace, a parliament. [pause]

So whether bilingualism reshapes the brain or merely accompanies privilege, and whether a dying tongue can truly be resurrected, both turn out to hinge less on linguistics than on institutions. And that pivot, naturally, is where the policymaker must enter — let me flag the key policy implication…
To conclude, then: preserving endangered languages and cultivating genuine bilingualism are not separate projects — they are, in essence, two sides of the same cognitive coin.

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~181 từ)
The chart compares the native speaker base of six languages in 2024 with their corresponding UNESCO language vitality scores, presented in two paired panels.

Overall, the two indicators appear to move broadly in tandem: languages with larger speaker populations tend to register higher vitality scores, whereas those with the smallest speaker bases sit at the bottom of the language endangerment scale. English, owing to its lingua franca status, occupies the top position on both measures.

In terms of speaker numbers, English led with 1,500 million speakers, followed by Mandarin at 1,100 million and Spanish at 550 million. These three commanded the lion's share of speakers and registered vitality scores of 9.5, 9.0 and 8.5 respectively, all firmly in the thriving range.

By contrast, Welsh, with under a million speakers, scored only 5.0, while Ainu, an indigenous minority dialect of Japan, recorded a mere 10,000 speakers and a critically low vitality of 1.0. Vietnamese occupied an intermediate position, with 85 million speakers and a healthy score of 7.5. The figures appear to suggest that demographic size and linguistic health are closely correlated.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~189 từ)
The chart sets the native speaker base of six languages in 2024 against their UNESCO vitality scores, the two metrics displayed in paired panels.

Overall, what emerges is a broadly positive association between demographic weight and linguistic health: the more numerous a language's speakers, the more robust its vitality, with the smallest tongues languishing at the foot of the endangerment scale. English, by virtue of its lingua franca status, crowns both rankings.

The three major languages dwarf the rest. English commanded a speaker base of 1,500 million, trailed by Mandarin at 1,100 million and Spanish at 550 million; their vitality scores of 9.5, 9.0 and 8.5 place them squarely in the thriving bracket. So commanding is English's base that it outnumbers Vietnamese roughly eighteenfold.

The smaller languages tell a starker story. Vietnamese, with 85 million speakers, still scored a healthy 7.5, yet Welsh, fewer than a million strong, managed only 5.0. Most striking of all is Ainu: with a mere 10,000 speakers, it registered a critically low 1.0, hovering on the brink of extinction. The data, then, lend tentative support to the view that size and survival are intertwined.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  B8 overview diễn đạt tương quan bằng cấu trúc 'the more ... the more' và động từ giàu hình ảnh ('languishing', 'crowns'), thay vì câu mô tả thẳng của B7.
•  B8 chèn so sánh bội số tường minh ('outnumbers Vietnamese roughly eighteenfold') và đảo ngữ ('So commanding is English's base that...'), nâng GRA + LR so với B7.
•  B8 đóng bằng hedging học thuật chuẩn xác hơn ('lend tentative support to the view that...') trong khi B7 chỉ kết 'closely correlated', cho thấy kiểm soát giọng điệu cao hơn.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Separate the two metrics: bars/left panel = speaker volumes, line/right panel = vitality scores.
•  Identify the correlation direction — broadly positive (more speakers, higher vitality) — and flag the critical case (Ainu at 1.0).
•  Highlight the extremes: English tops both panels, Ainu sits at the bottom of both.
•  Quantify both metrics for each language in the body paragraphs; never describe one axis without the other.
•  Close with a hedged correlation comment ('the figures appear to suggest a tentative link'), naming any exception.
T07 — LANGUAGE & LINGUISTICS · Writing Task 2
(1) Đề bài
Đề bài.  Many minority languages are disappearing. Some argue we should let them die out, while others say efforts should be made to preserve them. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
(2) Từ vựng chủ đề (Band 8 topic & argument lexis)

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
For letting minority languages die out:
•  Languages naturally evolve, merge and vanish; artificially propping up every dialect is futile, as Latin's transition shows.
•  Preservation programmes are a heavy financial burden whose resources could be redirected to healthcare or essential education.
•  A dominant lingua franca offers greater economic and labour-market value than a moribund minority dialect.
For preserving minority languages:
•  Languages encode unique ecological, medicinal and historical knowledge that vanishes with them.
•  Loss of a mother tongue equals loss of cultural identity; UNESCO frames it as a form of cultural genocide.
•  Revitalisation is demonstrably feasible — Welsh, Maori and Hebrew were all successfully revived through schooling and media.
(4) Gợi ý dàn bài — Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Conclusion
•  Introduction — paraphrase the dilemma over disappearing minority languages and state a leaning view toward preservation.
•  Body 1 — present the case for letting languages die out: natural evolution, financial burden, and the practicality of a lingua franca.
•  Body 2 — present the case for preservation and align the writer's opinion: encoded knowledge, cultural identity, and proven revival.
•  Conclusion — restate the qualified position favouring targeted, feasible preservation over passive acceptance.

rows: a language on the brink of extinction / a moribund tongue

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~273 words)

It is a striking fact that one minority language disappears roughly every two weeks. Whether such losses ought to be accepted as a natural evolution or actively resisted through preservation efforts is a question that divides linguists and policymakers. This essay will examine both views before arguing that determined preservation is, on balance, the wiser course.

Those who advocate letting minority languages die out argue that language extinction has always been part of human history. Latin, for example, gave way to the Romance languages without humanity being culturally impoverished by the change. From this perspective, attempting to artificially preserve every endangered dialect is a costly exercise that may yield little practical return. Furthermore, in an increasingly interconnected world, a young speaker of a minority tongue often gains far more economically from acquiring proficiency in a dominant lingua franca than from retaining a dialect of limited reach.

On the other hand, the case for preservation is, to my mind, the stronger one. Each language encodes unique ecological and historical knowledge; when it vanishes, that knowledge is lost forever. Moreover, a mother tongue is bound up with cultural identity, so its disappearance can inflict real psychological harm on a community. Crucially, revival is feasible rather than merely aspirational: Welsh, Maori and Hebrew have all been successfully revitalised through state-funded schooling, broadcasting and community language programmes.

In conclusion, although language death is sometimes a natural process, the cultural and intellectual cost of inaction is simply too high. Governments should therefore fund the targeted preservation of viable minority languages, prioritising those with a realistic prospect of survival, rather than allow them all to fall into extinction unchecked.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~284 words)

It is a sobering statistic that an indigenous language slips into extinction roughly every fortnight. Whether such attrition should be accepted as the natural churn of history or contested through deliberate preservation is a question that sharply divides scholars. My own position, on balance, is that selective preservation is amply justified, even if not every dialect can realistically be rescued.

There is, admittedly, a coherent case for non-intervention. Languages have always evolved, merged and died: Latin dissolved into the Romance tongues with no discernible loss to human civilisation, which suggests that propping up every moribund variety may be quixotic. Compounding this is the matter of cost; funds poured into reviving languages with a handful of elderly speakers might, some contend, be more humanely spent on healthcare or schooling. For the individual learner, moreover, fluency in a dominant lingua franca yields economic returns that a minority dialect simply cannot match.

Persuasive as these arguments are, they understate what is forfeited. Each language constitutes a unique repository of ecological and medicinal knowledge, much of it absent from any written archive; its loss is therefore irreversible. More fundamentally, a mother tongue is constitutive of cultural identity, which is precisely why UNESCO frames linguistic erasure as a form of cultural violence. And revival, far from being utopian, is demonstrable: were sustained funding married to grassroots transmission, even severely endangered languages could be resurrected, as Hebrew, Welsh and Maori attest.

In sum, while language death is partly inevitable, passive resignation is not the only response. The wiser course is to channel finite resources toward languages with a viable speaker community and a documented prospect of transmission, thereby preserving irreplaceable heritage without indulging in the futile fantasy of universal rescue.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  B8 mở bài bằng register cao ('a sobering statistic', 'the natural churn of history') và lập trường tinh tế ('selective preservation ... even if not every dialect can be rescued'), sâu hơn lập trường phẳng của B7.

•  B8 dùng nhượng bộ cao cấp ('Persuasive as these arguments are'), fronting ('Compounding this is the matter of cost') và đảo ngữ điều kiện ('were sustained funding married to...'), trong khi B7 dựa vào linkers cơ bản.

•  B8 chốt bằng tương phản học thuật ('preserving ... without indulging in futile universal rescue') và lexis chuẩn xác ('constitutive of cultural identity', 'a unique repository'), nâng LR + TR rõ rệt so với B7.

vocabulary.definition_vi: có nguy cơ biến mất, bị đe doạ tuyệt chủng
vocabulary.example: UNESCO's Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger lists hundreds of endangered languages that could vanish within a generation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'en-' (đặt vào) + 'danger' (nguy hiểm) → bị đặt vào tình trạng nguy hiểm, sắp biến mất.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phương ngữ, biến thể vùng miền của một ngôn ngữ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Regional **dialects** can differ so much in vocabulary and pronunciation that speakers sometimes struggle to understand one another.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Greek 'dia-' (giữa, qua lại) + 'lect' (nói) → cách nói riêng lưu hành giữa một nhóm người, một vùng.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'dialect' (biến thể vùng miền của CÙNG một ngôn ngữ) với 'language' (một hệ thống ngôn ngữ riêng biệt, thường không thông hiểu lẫn nhau).
vocabulary.definition_en: a particular form of a language spoken in a specific region or by a specific social group, differing in vocabulary, grammar or pronunciation
vocabulary.definition_vi: phương ngữ, tiếng địa phương
vocabulary.example: Regional dialects can differ so much in vocabulary and pronunciation that speakers sometimes struggle to understand one another.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Greek 'dia-' (giữa, qua lại) + 'lect' (nói) → cách nói riêng lưu hành giữa một nhóm người, một vùng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hùng biện, lưu loát và có sức thuyết phục khi nói hoặc viết.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The keynote speaker was so **eloquent** that the entire audience was captivated within minutes.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Latin 'e-' (ra ngoài) + 'loqui' (nói) → lời nói tuôn ra trôi chảy, cuốn hút.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'eloquent' (nói hay, thuyết phục) với 'elegant' (thanh lịch, tinh tế về hình thức).
vocabulary.definition_en: fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing, expressing ideas in a clear and impressive way
vocabulary.definition_vi: hùng biện, lưu loát và thuyết phục
vocabulary.example: The keynote speaker was so eloquent that the entire audience was captivated within minutes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Latin 'e-' (ra ngoài) + 'loqui' (nói) → lời nói tuôn ra trôi chảy, cuốn hút.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị xem xét, soi xét kỹ lưỡng, thường mang tính phản biện hoặc hoài nghi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> In recent years, the bilingual-advantage thesis has **come under** genuinely fierce **scrutiny** from replication studies.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'scrutiny' gốc Latin 'scrutari' (lục soát kỹ) → bị lục soát, xem xét từng chi tiết.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Scrutiny' là danh từ không đếm được, không dùng 'a scrutiny' hay 'scrutinies' theo nghĩa chung.
vocabulary.definition_en: to start being examined or questioned very closely and critically
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị xem xét, soi xét kỹ lưỡng (thường mang tính phản biện)
vocabulary.example: In recent years, the bilingual-advantage thesis has come under genuinely fierce scrutiny from replication studies.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'scrutiny' gốc Latin 'scrutari' (lục soát kỹ) → bị lục soát, xem xét từng chi tiết.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật lộn, cố gắng đấu tranh để giải quyết hoặc hiểu một vấn đề khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Even the world's most advanced AI translation tools still **grapple with** cultural nuances and idiomatic humour.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'grapple' vốn nghĩa 'móc, ghì chặt' (như trong đấu vật) → vật lộn để xử lý vấn đề khó.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Grapple' luôn cần giới từ 'with' khi mang nghĩa 'vật lộn với vấn đề': không nói 'grapple a problem'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to struggle to deal with or understand a difficult problem or issue
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn, đấu tranh để giải quyết (một vấn đề khó khăn)
vocabulary.example: Even the world's most advanced AI translation tools still grapple with cultural nuances and idiomatic humour.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grapple' vốn nghĩa 'móc, ghì chặt' (như trong đấu vật) → vật lộn để xử lý vấn đề khó.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiện tượng lỗi sai ăn sâu, cố định và rất khó sửa ở người học ngoại ngữ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Adult learners frequently plateau, and unless corrected early, their errors risk **fossilisation**, becoming almost impossible to remediate.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'fossil' (hoá thạch, thứ cứng lại vĩnh viễn) → lỗi sai cũng 'cứng lại', khó thay đổi.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm nghĩa ngôn ngữ học của 'fossilisation' (lỗi ăn sâu ở người học ngoại ngữ) với nghĩa sinh học gốc (hoá thạch).
vocabulary.definition_en: the permanent entrenchment of errors in a second-language learner's speech or writing, which become highly resistant to correction
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự hoá thạch lỗi (lỗi sai ăn sâu, khó sửa khi học ngoại ngữ)
vocabulary.example: Adult learners frequently plateau, and unless corrected early, their errors risk fossilisation, becoming almost impossible to remediate.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'fossil' (hoá thạch, thứ cứng lại vĩnh viễn) → lỗi sai cũng 'cứng lại', khó thay đổi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuyết tương đối ngôn ngữ, cho rằng cấu trúc ngôn ngữ ảnh hưởng đến cách người nói tư duy.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The weaker version of **linguistic relativity** retains considerable empirical support, as speakers of languages with finer colour vocabularies distinguish hues more rapidly.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'relativity' (tính tương đối, như thuyết của Einstein) áp vào ngôn ngữ → tư duy 'tương đối' theo ngôn ngữ mẹ đẻ.
collocations: a moderated version of linguistic relativity
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm phiên bản 'mạnh' (ngôn ngữ quyết định hoàn toàn tư duy, đã bị bác bỏ) với phiên bản 'yếu' (ngôn ngữ chỉ định hướng, có bằng chứng thực nghiệm) của giả thuyết này.
vocabulary.definition_en: the hypothesis, associated with Sapir and Whorf, that the structure of a language influences how its speakers perceive and think about the world
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuyết tương đối ngôn ngữ (giả thuyết Sapir-Whorf: ngôn ngữ định hình tư duy)
vocabulary.example: The weaker version of linguistic relativity retains considerable empirical support, as speakers of languages with finer colour vocabularies distinguish hues more rapidly.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'relativity' (tính tương đối, như thuyết của Einstein) áp vào ngôn ngữ → tư duy 'tương đối' theo ngôn ngữ mẹ đẻ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hấp hối, sắp tàn lụi — chỉ còn rất ít người dùng và gần như không còn khả năng tồn tại.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A **moribund** language typically has only elderly speakers and a thin documentary record, unlike a fully extinct one.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Latin 'mori' (chết) → moribund → đang trên đà chết dần, hấp hối.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'moribund' (vẫn còn vài người nói, sắp tuyệt chủng) với 'extinct' (đã hoàn toàn không còn ai nói).
vocabulary.definition_en: (of a language, institution or practice) in terminal decline, with very few remaining users and little prospect of survival
vocabulary.definition_vi: hấp hối, sắp tàn lụi (chỉ còn rất ít người dùng, sắp biến mất)
vocabulary.example: A moribund language typically has only elderly speakers and a thin documentary record, unlike a fully extinct one.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Latin 'mori' (chết) → moribund → đang trên đà chết dần, hấp hối.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự linh hoạt trong nhận thức, khả năng chuyển đổi tư duy để thích nghi với tình huống mới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> APA-published meta-analyses confirm that bilinguals exhibit enhanced **cognitive flexibility** compared with monolingual peers.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'cognitive' (thuộc về nhận thức) + 'flexibility' (linh hoạt, dẻo) → tư duy uyển chuyển, dễ thích nghi.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Cognitive flexibility' là một thuật ngữ tâm lý học cố định; tránh dịch máy móc thành 'sự dẻo dai nhận thức' gây tối nghĩa.
vocabulary.definition_en: the mental ability to switch between different concepts or tasks and adapt thinking to new, unexpected situations
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự linh hoạt nhận thức (khả năng chuyển đổi tư duy linh hoạt)
vocabulary.example: APA-published meta-analyses confirm that bilinguals exhibit enhanced cognitive flexibility compared with monolingual peers.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'cognitive' (thuộc về nhận thức) + 'flexibility' (linh hoạt, dẻo) → tư duy uyển chuyển, dễ thích nghi.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự bá quyền ngôn ngữ, khi một ngôn ngữ thống trị mang lại lợi thế bất công cho người bản ngữ của nó.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Dominant as English currently is, the **linguistic hegemony** it enjoys is, by some accounts, already being eroded by the rise of Mandarin and AI translation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Greek 'hegemon' (người lãnh đạo, thống trị) → linguistic hegemony → một ngôn ngữ 'lãnh đạo', áp đảo các ngôn ngữ khác.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Hegemony' phát âm là /hɪˈɡem.ə.ni/, trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết thứ hai, không phải /ˈhedʒ.ə.məʊ.ni/ như nhiều người đọc nhầm.
vocabulary.definition_en: the dominance of one language over others, often giving its native speakers disproportionate social, economic or political advantage
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự bá quyền ngôn ngữ (một ngôn ngữ thống trị, gây bất lợi cho ngôn ngữ khác)
vocabulary.example: Dominant as English currently is, the linguistic hegemony it enjoys is, by some accounts, already being eroded by the rise of Mandarin and AI translation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Greek 'hegemon' (người lãnh đạo, thống trị) → linguistic hegemony → một ngôn ngữ 'lãnh đạo', áp đảo các ngôn ngữ khác.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hiểu lầm nhau, mỗi người theo đuổi một ý khác nhau mà không nhận ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We didn't agree on the plan because we were clearly talking **at cross purposes**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'cross' (chéo nhau, trái ngược) + 'purposes' (mục đích) → hai bên có mục đích/ý hiểu chéo nhau, không khớp.
collocations: be at cross purposes with someone
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn ở số nhiều 'purposes' trong thành ngữ này; không nói 'at cross purpose'.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of two or more people) misunderstanding or having different intentions in a conversation without realising it, leading to confusion
vocabulary.definition_vi: hiểu lầm nhau, mỗi người nói một ý (do không hiểu ý nhau)
vocabulary.example: We didn't agree on the plan because we were clearly talking at cross purposes.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'cross' (chéo nhau, trái ngược) + 'purposes' (mục đích) → hai bên có mục đích/ý hiểu chéo nhau, không khớp.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tiếng mẹ đẻ, ngôn ngữ đầu tiên một người học được từ nhỏ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Although she has lived in France for twenty years, Vietnamese is still her **mother tongue**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'mother' (mẹ) + 'tongue' (lưỡi, tiếng nói) → ngôn ngữ học được từ mẹ, từ thuở lọt lòng.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng làm tính từ ghép trước danh từ, cần gạch nối: 'a mother-tongue speaker', không viết rời 'mother tongue speaker'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the language a person learns first as a child and typically speaks most naturally
vocabulary.definition_vi: tiếng mẹ đẻ
vocabulary.example: Although she has lived in France for twenty years, Vietnamese is still her mother tongue.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'mother' (mẹ) + 'tongue' (lưỡi, tiếng nói) → ngôn ngữ học được từ mẹ, từ thuở lọt lòng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị mất đi sắc thái hoặc ý nghĩa gốc khi được dịch sang ngôn ngữ khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The movie's subtle humour was completely **lost in translation** when it was dubbed into another language.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Ý tưởng như một vật bị 'thất lạc' (lost) trên hành trình chuyển ngữ (translation) → không đến được đích nguyên vẹn.
vocabulary.common_error: Thành ngữ này dùng dạng bị động cố định 'be/get lost in translation'; không chia động từ 'lose' theo chủ ngữ chủ động.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of meaning, humour or nuance) failing to be conveyed accurately when text or speech is translated from one language to another
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị mất nghĩa/sắc thái khi dịch (dịch không lột tả được ý gốc)
vocabulary.example: The movie's subtle humour was completely lost in translation when it was dubbed into another language.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Ý tưởng như một vật bị 'thất lạc' (lost) trên hành trình chuyển ngữ (translation) → không đến được đích nguyên vẹn.
